summary:
ORBITAL — Space Mission Design & Simulation Game

ORBITAL is an interactive, browser-based space mission design and simulation game created for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Stepping into the role of a flight director at a space agency, players architect robotic exploration missions to five authentic planetary destinations: the Moon, Mars, Earth orbit, Asteroid 16 Psyche, and Europa.

Rather than presenting a passive dashboard, ORBITAL challenges players with real aerospace engineering trade-offs. Every decision carries physical and operational consequences. Players select launch vehicles (such as Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, or SLS), mount specialized science sensors, and configure power generation, energy storage, communications, and thermal protection against a strict budget. Authentic mechanics—including the inverse-square law for solar flux, payload fairing mass limits, and interplanetary communications latency—directly dictate mission feasibility.

Before launch, an automated pre-flight matrix validates engineering tolerances. During the 6-phase live simulation, players track telemetry in real time and confront unexpected orbital anomalies, from solar particle storms to optical dust deposition. Tactical decisions shape final probe survival and scientific yield. 

ORBITAL transforms real NASA planetary science into an engaging, hands-on engineering game where every choice matters.
details:
ORBITAL is an interactive browser-based space mission engineering simulator and game created for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Players assume the role of a space agency flight director tasked with designing, validating, and executing robotic exploration missions across the solar system. The workflow begins by selecting a destination from five authentic planetary profiles, including the Moon, Mars, Earth orbit, Asteroid 16 Psyche, and Europa, followed by defining mission scientific objectives. Players then enter an interactive spacecraft builder to select real-world launch vehicles, such as Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, or the Space Launch System, and configure subsystems including scientific instruments, solar arrays or nuclear power generators, battery buffers, deep-space communications, propulsion engines, thermal shielding, and navigation gear. An integrated pre-flight matrix validates engineering constraints before clearing the spacecraft for flight. Once launched, a live six-phase simulation progresses through flight stages, confronting players with random orbital anomalies that demand tactical decisions affecting probe survival and scientific yield.

The primary benefit of the project is demystifying complex aerospace engineering trade-offs by turning abstract equations into intuitive, hands-on cause-and-effect learning. Players directly witness the consequences of their design choices, learning firsthand why mounting more scientific instruments requires larger launch vehicles, or how power generation demands change drastically based on distance from the Sun. By running completely in any modern web browser without installations, user logins, or fees, it provides zero-barrier access to aerospace education. Replayability is exceptionally high due to diverse destination constraints, customizable payloads, and unpredictable flight events that challenge players to optimize their designs under varying difficulty modes.

The intended impact of ORBITAL is to inspire students, educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide by illustrating how physics, math, economics, and engineering intersect in planetary exploration. By grounding every mission in authentic NASA planetary exploration science, including missions like the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Psyche, and Europa Clipper, ORBITAL fosters broader public appreciation for space science and systems engineering. It is designed to serve as an accessible educational tool for classrooms and STEM programs exploring orbital mechanics, resource management, and aerospace design.

The project was developed entirely using a modern web development stack consisting of React, Vite, modern JavaScript, and React Router. Visualizations and interactive components were built using Three.js for procedural 3D modeling of multi-stage launch vehicles and spacecraft buses, combined with HTML5 Canvas for an interactive spring-physics constellation starfield. Recharts was used to render resource telemetry curves, Lucide React provided technical iconography, and Tailwind CSS powered a responsive dark-mode aerospace mission control user interface. The simulation engine is written in pure modular JavaScript without external backend dependencies, utilizing browser local storage for persistent flight logs. Science data and planetary parameters were calibrated using public NASA Planetary Science Division documentation and NASA Open APIs.

The creativity of ORBITAL lies in blending high-fidelity 3D computer-aided design visualization with authentic physical simulation mechanics. Rather than relying on static illustrations or arbitrary hit points, ORBITAL visually reconstructs full multi-stage rockets and custom spacecraft that update in real time as components are swapped. It faithfully implements real physical laws, such as the inverse-square law for solar irradiance and speed-of-light communications delay. Furthermore, its live simulation introduces branching narrative dilemmas during space weather events, where players must make split-second tactical decisions to protect their spacecraft or risk equipment degradation for bonus scientific discovery.

Throughout development, the team prioritized striking the ideal balance between scientific authenticity and intuitive gameplay, translating rigorous orbital physics, delta-V requirements, and telemetry margins into clear, actionable cockpit metrics. The team carefully modeled interdependent trade-offs where every component choice ripples across budget, wet mass, electrical balance, and downlink throughput. Universal cross-platform accessibility and performance were also paramount considerations, ensuring the application runs smoothly on standard laptops, tablets, and mobile devices without requiring logins, installations, or paid third-party infrastructure.
